title: Capstone Engineering Lab: End-to-End Predictive Maintenance
text:
In this final integrative lab, you will take the Industrial Motor Telemetry Dataset (vibration_mm_s, temp_c, current_amp, acoustic_db) and execute a unified 4-Module AI & Data Science Pipeline in a single runnable script. Use this template as the foundation for your 15-Mark Course Microproject!



Module 4 (Data Science Process): Cleanse missing values, standardize the 4 sensor channels, and perform a stratified Train/Test split.
Module 2 (Linear Algebra — SVD & PCA): Decompose the training covariance matrix via SVD (\(X = USV^T\)) and project the 4D sensors onto a 2D Principal Component health space.
Module 3 (Probability & Statistics — MLE, Bayes & OLS): Estimate class-conditional Gaussian parameters via MLE, fit a Bayesian classifier, and compute the Least Squares Regression line between motor current and winding temperature.
Module 1 (Machine Learning & Deep Neural Networks): Train K-Means, Logistic Regression, and a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLPClassifier) on both the full 4D space and the 2D PCA-compressed space, comparing their diagnostic accuracy!
crumbs: Capstone Engineering Lab: End-to-End Predictive Maintenance

title: Day 2, Session 3: Applied Probability & Statistical Estimation
section: 2 1. Random Variables, Statistical Summaries & Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)
text:
2 1. Random Variables, Statistical Summaries & Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)
Suppose we model a continuous feature \(X\) (such as Iris petal_length within a species) as a Gaussian (Normal) Random Variable \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with probability density function (PDF):
\[f(x \mid \mu, \sigma^2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \sigma^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\]
Given \(n\) independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) observations \(\{x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n\}\), how do we estimate the unknown parameters \(\theta = (\mu, \sigma^2)\)?

Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE): We write the Likelihood Function \(L(\mu, \sigma^2) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i \mid \mu, \sigma^2)\) and maximize its natural logarithm, the Log-Likelihood \(\ell(\mu, \sigma^2) = \ln L(\mu, \sigma^2)\):
\[\ell(\mu, \sigma^2) = -\frac{n}{2}\ln(2\pi) - \frac{n}{2}\ln(\sigma^2) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \mu)^2\]
Setting the partial derivatives \(\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \mu} = 0\) and \(\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial (\sigma^2)} = 0\) yields the closed-form MLE Estimators:
\[\hat{\mu}_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i, \qquad \hat{\sigma}^2_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \hat{\mu}_{\text{MLE}})^2\]

Let’s verify this both analytically and by plotting the Log-Likelihood surface on the Iris dataset!
crumbs: Day 2, Session 3: Applied Probability & Statistical Estimation

title: Day 2, Session 3: Applied Probability & Statistical Estimation
section: 3 2. Bayes’ Theorem and Its AI Application: Gaussian Naive Bayes
text:
3 2. Bayes’ Theorem and Its AI Application: Gaussian Naive Bayes
Once we have estimated the class-conditional likelihoods \(P(X \mid C_k)\) via MLE, how do we flip the conditioning to predict the posterior probability of class \(C_k\) given a new measurement \(x\)? We apply Bayes’ Theorem:
\[P(C_k \mid x) = \frac{P(x \mid C_k) \, P(C_k)}{P(x)} = \frac{P(x \mid C_k) \, P(C_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K P(x \mid C_j) \, P(C_j)}\]

Prior \(P(C_k)\): Base rate of class \(k\) before seeing the features (\(1/3\) each in Iris).
Likelihood \(P(x \mid C_k)\): Evaluated from our MLE Gaussian density \(\prod_{j=1}^d \mathcal{N}(x_j \mid \hat{\mu}_{kj}, \hat{\sigma}^2_{kj})\).
Posterior \(P(C_k \mid x)\): Exact probability that flower \(x\) belongs to species \(C_k\)!

title: Day 2, Session 3: Applied Probability & Statistical Estimation
section: 4 3. Linear Correlation (\(r\)) & Least Squares Linear Regression (OLS)
text:
4 3. Linear Correlation (\(r\)) & Least Squares Linear Regression (OLS)
In engineering and data science, we frequently need to quantify the linear association between two continuous variables \((X, Y)\) and predict \(Y\) from \(X\).

1. Karl Pearson’s Coefficient of Linear Correlation (\(r\)): \[r = \frac{\text{Cov}(X, Y)}{\sigma_X \sigma_Y} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2} \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar{y})^2}} \in [-1, +1]\]
2. Linear Regression via Method of Least Squares (OLS): We fit the line \(\hat{y}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\) by minimizing the Residual Sum of Squares (RSS): \[\text{RSS}(\beta_0, \beta_1) = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i))^2\] Setting \(\frac{\partial \text{RSS}}{\partial \beta_0} = 0\) and \(\frac{\partial \text{RSS}}{\partial \beta_1} = 0\) gives the normal equations with closed-form solution: \[\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2} = r \frac{s_Y}{s_X}, \qquad \hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta}_1 \bar{x}\]

2.1 Key Challenges in Machine Learning (Géron, Ch. 1)

Data Challenges: Insufficient quantity of training data, non-representative training data (sampling bias), poor-quality data (noise, missing values), and irrelevant features (garbage in, garbage out).
Algorithm Challenges:

Underfitting (High Bias): Model is too simple to capture underlying structure (e.g., fitting a linear boundary to non-linear data). Remedy: more complex model, better features, less regularization.
Overfitting (High Variance): Model memorizes training noise and fails to generalize to unseen test data. Remedy: regularization (\(L_1/L_2\)), more training data, early stopping.

title: Day 2, Session 4: Machine Learning Systems & Deep Neural Networks
section: 3 2. Unsupervised Learning: K-Means Clustering
text:
3 2. Unsupervised Learning: K-Means Clustering
Given unlabeled points \(\{x_1, \dots, x_n\} \subset \mathbb{R}^d\), K-Means partitions the data into \(K\) clusters \(C_1, \dots, C_K\) with centroids \(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_K\) to minimize the Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (Inertia \(J\)):
\[J(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_K) = \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{x_i \in C_k} \|x_i - \mu_k\|_2^2\]
It alternates two steps until convergence: 1. Assignment Step: Assign each point \(x_i\) to its nearest centroid: \(c^{(i)} = \arg\min_k \|x_i - \mu_k\|_2^2\). 2. Update Step: Recompute each centroid as the mean of its assigned points: \(\mu_k = \frac{1}{|C_k|}\sum_{x_i \in C_k} x_i\).
crumbs: Day 2, Session 4: Machine Learning Systems & Deep Neural Networks

title: Day 2, Session 4: Machine Learning Systems & Deep Neural Networks
section: 4 3. Supervised Classification: Logistic Regression
text:
4 3. Supervised Classification: Logistic Regression
Despite its name, Logistic Regression is a probabilistic classification model. For binary classification, it passes the linear score (logit) \(z = w^T x + b\) through the Logistic Sigmoid function \(\sigma(z)\):
\[\hat{p} = P(y=1 \mid x) = \sigma(w^T x + b) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(w^T x + b)}} \in (0, 1)\]
For \(K > 2\) classes (Multinomial Logistic Regression / Softmax), we compute \(z_k = w_k^T x + b_k\) and apply the Softmax function:
\[P(y=k \mid x) = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{j=1}^K e^{z_j}}\]
Parameters \((W, b)\) are trained by minimizing the Cross-Entropy Loss (which is equivalent to Maximum Likelihood Estimation from Module 3!).
crumbs: Day 2, Session 4: Machine Learning Systems & Deep Neural Networks

title: Day 2, Session 4: Machine Learning Systems & Deep Neural Networks
section: 5 4. Artificial Neural Networks: Perceptron, UAT & Deep MLPs
text:
5 4. Artificial Neural Networks: Perceptron, UAT & Deep MLPs

5.1 The Perceptron (Rosenblatt, 1957)
A Perceptron is the simplest artificial neuron. It computes a weighted sum of inputs plus a bias, \(z = w^T x + b = \sum_{j=1}^d w_j x_j + b\), and applies a Heaviside step activation function:
\[\hat{y} = \text{step}(z) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } w^T x + b \ge 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } w^T x + b < 0 \end{cases}\]
Limitation (Minsky & Papert, 1969): A single-layer Perceptron can only learn linearly separable patterns (it cannot solve the XOR problem).


5.2 Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) & Deep Neural Networks (DNN)
By stacking one or more hidden layers of neurons with non-linear activation functions \(g(\cdot)\) (such as ReLU \(g(z) = \max(0, z)\), Sigmoid \(\sigma(z)\), or Tanh \(\tanh(z)\)), we form a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). When an MLP has multiple hidden layers, it is called a Deep Neural Network (DNN):
\[h^{(1)} = g\big(W^{(1)} x + b^{(1)}\big), \quad h^{(2)} = g\big(W^{(2)} h^{(1)} + b^{(2)}\big), \quad \hat{y} = \text{Output}\big(W^{(3)} h^{(2)} + b^{(3)}\big)\]

Universal Approximation Theorem (Statement Only — Syllabus Requirement): A feedforward neural network (Multi-Layer Perceptron) with a single hidden layer containing a finite number of neurons and a continuous, non-polynomial activation function (such as sigmoid or ReLU) can approximate any continuous function \(f: K \subset \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^m\) on a compact subset \(K\) of \(\mathbb{R}^d\) to any desired degree of accuracy \(\varepsilon > 0\), provided sufficient hidden units are available.



5.3 Syllabus Demonstration: Both Regression and Classification using MLP
In the interactive code block below, we demonstrate both syllabus problems using Multi-Layer Perceptrons on the Iris dataset: 1. MLP Regression (MLPRegressor): Using sepal_length, sepal_width, and petal_length (\(\mathbb{R}^3\)) to predict continuous petal_width (\(\mathbb{R}\)), evaluated via RMSE and \(R^2\). 2. MLP Classification (MLPClassifier): Using a Deep Neural Network with two hidden layers (16, 8) and ReLU activations to classify all 3 Iris species, plotting the training loss convergence curve!

title: Day 1, Session 2: Mathematical Foundations — Linear Algebra, SVD & PCA
section: 2 1. Mean-Centering and the Covariance Matrix \(\Sigma\)
text:
2 1. Mean-Centering and the Covariance Matrix \(\Sigma\)
Let \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) be our standardized (or mean-centered) data matrix where each column has mean \(0\). The sample covariance matrix \(\Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\) captures both the variance of each feature (diagonal entries) and the linear redundancy between features (off-diagonal entries):
\[\Sigma = \frac{1}{n - 1} X^T X\]
Notice two critical properties of \(\Sigma\): 1. \(\Sigma\) is a square \(d \times d\) matrix (\(4 \times 4\) for Iris and Motor sensors). 2. \(\Sigma\) is real and symmetric (\(\Sigma^T = \Sigma\)) and positive semi-definite (\(v^T \Sigma v \ge 0\)).

title: Day 1, Session 2: Mathematical Foundations — Linear Algebra, SVD & PCA
section: 3 2. Spectral Decomposition (Eigendecomposition)
text:
3 2. Spectral Decomposition (Eigendecomposition)
By the Spectral Theorem, any real symmetric matrix \(\Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\) can be factored into an orthogonal matrix of eigenvectors \(Q\) and a diagonal matrix of real eigenvalues \(\Lambda\):
\[\Sigma = Q \Lambda Q^T = \sum_{i=1}^d \lambda_i q_i q_i^T\]
where: * \(q_1, q_2, \dots, q_d\) are mutually orthonormal eigenvectors (\(q_i^T q_j = \delta_{ij}\), so \(Q^T Q = I\)). Geometrically, these define the principal axes of variance of the data cloud! * \(\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_d \ge 0\) are the corresponding eigenvalues, which measure the exact variance of the data projected onto each axis \(q_i\).
crumbs: Day 1, Session 2: Mathematical Foundations — Linear Algebra, SVD & PCA

title: Day 1, Session 2: Mathematical Foundations — Linear Algebra, SVD & PCA
section: 4 3. Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)
text:
4 3. Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)
What if we don’t even want to form \(X^T X\) (which can lose numerical precision)? Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) factors any rectangular matrix \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) directly:
\[X = U S V^T\]

\(U \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\): Orthogonal matrix of left singular vectors (columns are eigenvectors of \(X X^T\)).
\(S \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\): Diagonal matrix of non-negative singular values \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_d \ge 0\).
\(V \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\): Orthogonal matrix of right singular vectors (columns are eigenvectors of \(X^T X\)).


The Golden Bridge Connecting SVD, Spectral Decomposition, and PCA: Substitute \(X = U S V^T\) into the covariance formula \(\Sigma = \frac{1}{n-1} X^T X\): \[\Sigma = \frac{1}{n-1} (U S V^T)^T (U S V^T) = \frac{1}{n-1} V S^T U^T U S V^T = V \left(\frac{S^2}{n-1}\right) V^T\] Comparing this with \(\Sigma = Q \Lambda Q^T\), we see immediately that: 1. The right singular vectors \(V\) are identical to the spectral eigenvectors \(Q\) (the Principal Components!). 2. The eigenvalues \(\lambda_i\) of the covariance matrix are directly related to the singular values \(\sigma_i\): \[\lambda_i = \frac{\sigma_i^2}{n - 1}\]

title: Day 1, Session 2: Mathematical Foundations — Linear Algebra, SVD & PCA
section: 5 4. Dimensionality Reduction via Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
text:
5 4. Dimensionality Reduction via Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
To project our \(d\)-dimensional data matrix \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) down to a \(k\)-dimensional subspace (\(k < d\), e.g., \(k=2\)), we simply multiply \(X\) by the first \(k\) columns of \(V\) (let’s call this \(W_k = V_{:, 1:k} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}\)):
\[Z = X W_k \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}\]
And we can reconstruct the low-rank approximation \(\hat{X}_k \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) back in the original 4D space via:
\[\hat{X}_k = Z W_k^T = \sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i u_i v_i^T\]
By the Eckart-Young-Mirsky Theorem, \(\hat{X}_k\) is the best rank-\(k\) approximation to \(X\) in Frobenius norm! Let’s visualize the 2D PCA projection of Iris alongside the Scree Plot (cumulative variance explained):

section: 2 1. The 6-Step Data Science Process (Cielen & Meysman)
text:
2 1. The 6-Step Data Science Process (Cielen & Meysman)
In Introducing Data Science (Text-5), the lifecycle of any data science or engineering AI project follows six iterative stages:

Setting the Research Goal: Define the problem, context, deliverable, and success metrics (e.g., Can we classify flower species or detect motor bearing wear with \(>95\%\) accuracy?).
Retrieving Data: Collect internal/external data from databases, CSV logs, or IoT sensors.
Data Preparation (Cleansing, Transforming, Combining): Handle missing values (NaN), outliers, unit mismatches, and feature scaling (\(z\)-score standardization).
Data Exploration (EDA): Compute statistical summaries, plot histograms, boxplots, scatter matrices, and correlation heatmaps to spot patterns and anomalies.
Data Modeling (Statistics + Machine Learning): Select features, split into Training and Testing sets, fit statistical/ML models, and evaluate generalization error.
Presentation & Automation: Communicate findings via dashboards (Tableau, PowerBI, Quarto) or deploy automated real-time inference pipelines.

3 2. Primary Thread: Exploring & Preparing the Iris Data Matrix
Every dataset in AI starts as a feature matrix \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) and (for supervised tasks) a target vector \(y \in \mathbb{R}^n\):
\[X = \begin{bmatrix} x_{11} & x_{12} & \dots & x_{1d} \\ x_{21} & x_{22} & \dots & x_{2d} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ x_{n1} & x_{n2} & \dots & x_{nd} \end{bmatrix}, \quad y = \begin{bmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \\ \vdots \\ y_n \end{bmatrix}\]
For the Iris dataset, \(n = 150\) flowers and \(d = 4\) continuous morphological measurements (in cm). Notice how features have different scales and variances—which is why Step 3 (Data Preparation) requires Standardization (\(z\)-score scaling):
\[z_{ij} = \frac{x_{ij} - \mu_j}{\sigma_j}\]
